towns:Calella de Palafrugell and Llafran.name: Calella de Palafrugell and Llafranc
towns:Calella de Palafrugell and Llafran.teaser: Two coves of Palafrugell, a cliff path between them, and a lighthouse on the headland above
towns:Calella de Palafrugell and Llafran.story: Palafrugell itself sits inland; its sea is three coves, and these are the two that matter most. Calella is the fishermen's one: small beaches split by rocks, boats pulled up on the sand, white houses built almost into the water. Llafranc, over the headland, is a single curved bay with a short promenade and a marina, watched from above by the Sant Sebastià lighthouse. A cliff path joins them in well under two hours. In mid-October the coves are emptying, the sea is still swimmable on calm days, and the first tramuntana days blow the haze off the Medes. Some seasonal places shut from late October.
towns:Calella de Palafrugell and Llafran.why: Come in autumn, when you can walk the whole front of Calella and hear only the boats knocking on their moorings.

towns:Palamós.name: Palamós
towns:Palamós.teaser: A port that still works for a living: trawlers in by late afternoon, red prawns on the quay, a fishing museum
towns:Palamós.story: Most of this coast lives off visitors; Palamós still lives off its boats. The trawlers go out before dawn to the deep canyon offshore and come back in the afternoon with the gamba de Palamós, the deep-red prawn that carries a guaranteed-origin mark. The catch is sold in the llotja on the fishing quay, and next to it the Museu de la Pesca tells the story of the fleet, from sail to diesel. Each late spring the certified restaurants run the Menú de la Gamba; in 2026 the Fira de la Gamba filled the fish hall on 13 June. By October the town is back to working pace.
towns:Palamós.why: Stand on the Moll Pesquer when the boats come in: you see the prawn before any kitchen does.

towns:Pals and Peratallada.name: Pals and Peratallada
towns:Pals and Peratallada.teaser: Two medieval villages of golden stone a few kilometres apart, with rice fields running out towards the sea
towns:Pals and Peratallada.story: Pals stands on a hill above the flat Baix Ter plain: steep lanes, stone arches, and below it the paddies that have made its name. Rice has been grown here since at least the 15th century, banned in the 19th over fears of fever from the standing water, and brought back in the early 20th, largely by Pere Coll i Rigau. Peratallada, a short drive inland, is lower and tighter, a knot of streets around a porticoed square; its name means carved stone. Both villages fill up on summer weekends. A weekday in October gives you the stone, the light and the lanes almost to yourself.
towns:Pals and Peratallada.why: See both in one morning and end with a long lunch under the arcades of Peratallada.
facts: Two walled stone villages and the rice plain between them and the sea

towns:L'Escala and Empúries.name: L'Escala and Empúries
towns:L'Escala and Empúries.teaser: An anchovy town with Greek and Roman ruins at the end of its seafront path
towns:L'Escala and Empúries.story: L'Escala is a fishing town that learned to keep its catch. Salt was its currency for centuries, stored in the Alfolí de la Sal, finished in 1697, and the anchovy trade grew from it; two old houses still work by hand, Callol i Serrats from 1847 and Solés. The Museu de l'Anxova i de la Sal, on Avinguda Francesc Macià, puts the tools and the boats on show. North of town a promenade runs along the shore through pines to the ruins of Empúries and the tiny walled village of Sant Martí. In October the beaches are empty and the town's own people are back on the benches.
towns:L'Escala and Empúries.why: Walk out to the ruins in the morning and back into town for anchovies on bread at noon.

towns:Roses.name: Roses
towns:Roses.teaser: A wide bay, a star-shaped fortress older than the resort around it, and a five-table counter for fish
towns:Roses.story: Roses is the big beach town at the head of its gulf, and in summer it looks it. Look past the apartments. At the western edge of town sits the Ciutadella, a walled pentagon from the 16th century that encloses far older ground: the remains of Greek Rhode, a medieval monastery and the fort's own ruins, now run by the town as a heritage site. On the point to the east stands the Castell de la Trinitat. The fishing fleet still lands in the port, which is why the town's best table is a counter grilling what came in that morning. Autumn shrinks it back to size.
towns:Roses.why: Give the Ciutadella an hour: inside the walls you walk through twenty-five centuries in one field.
facts: The bay, the walled Ciutadella, and fish off the boats

towns:Cadaqués and Portlligat.name: Cadaqués and Portlligat
towns:Cadaqués and Portlligat.teaser: The white village behind the cape, and Dalí's bay over the hill: Cadaqués has its own guide
towns:Cadaqués and Portlligat.story: Cadaqués is the whitewashed fishing village on the far side of the Cap de Creus massif, reached by one winding road over the hills from Roses, which kept it apart long enough to draw painters. Portlligat, a few minutes' walk north over the rise, is the small bay where Dalí lived and worked. Both deserve more than a stop on the way somewhere else, so they have their own guide, with its walks, coves, tables and larder. From this coast, plan at least a full day, and watch the forecast: a strong tramuntana makes the road and the cape hard going.

towns:Girona.name: Girona
towns:Girona.teaser: The medieval city on the Onyar, its Jewish quarter and the kitchens that brought cooks from everywhere
towns:Girona.story: Forty minutes inland from the coast, Girona is a walled city climbing a hill above the Onyar river. The Barri Vell, the old town, is a tangle of stone steps and lanes under the cathedral; inside it lies El Call, the medieval Jewish quarter, one of the best kept in Europe, all narrow passages and courtyards. Along the river the houses hang over the water in ochre, rust and cream, colours chosen when the fronts were restored in 1983-84. The city also holds one of the world's most famous restaurants and a cluster of tables around it. Girona has its own guide, which tells it all properly.
towns:Girona.why: Girona has its own guide: come for a day from the coast, and stay for dinner if you have the booking.

curiosities:Named on 12 September 1908.name: Named on 12 September 1908
curiosities:Named on 12 September 1908.teaser: The coast got its name in a newspaper column signed 'Pol', and not everyone accepts the credit
curiosities:Named on 12 September 1908.story: On 12 September 1908 the journalist and politician Ferran Agulló published a piece called 'Per la Costa Brava' in the Barcelona daily La Veu de Catalunya, signed with his pen name, Pol. It is the first known printed use of the name for this coast, and it meant wild or rugged, not brave. The name spread the next year, when a cruise sold as a trip along the 'costa brava catalana' put it into wider use. How much shore Agulló meant is unclear: some read it as the cliffs from Blanes to Begur, others as everything from the Tordera river to Cap de Creus and beyond.
curiosities:Named on 12 September 1908.why: Brava here means rugged: say it that way and you will sound like you read the original column.
facts: The article is reprinted in Marines, a collection of Agulló's sea writing edited by Pep Vila (Curbet Edicions)

Josep Pla questioned the credit and placed the name's origin at the Hotel Paradís in Fornells, Begur; the Gran Enciclopèdia Catalana dates the coinage to 1905; and the phrase was already used for a stretch of Mallorca's north coast

curiosities:The wind that plants the vin.name: The wind that plants the vines low
curiosities:The wind that plants the vin.teaser: The tramuntana has topped 200 km/h at Portbou, and it decides how every Empordà vine is grown
curiosities:The wind that plants the vin.story: The tramuntana is a cold north wind that pours off the Pyrenees and down across the Empordà, sometimes for days at a stretch. Gusts above 100 km/h are routine in a strong episode; the highest recorded at Portbou reached 218 km/h, on 29 January 2001. Growers learned to work with it. A vine left tall would be torn, so they keep it low, as a short bush tied to a stake. The wind pays back the trouble: it dries the leaves after rain and dew, so mildew and powdery mould rarely take hold, and the grapes stay small and concentrated. From now until spring is its season.
curiosities:The wind that plants the vin.why: Drive the vineyard roads on a tramuntana day and watch the low bushes take a gale that bends the cypresses flat.
facts: Any old vineyard of the Alt Empordà, around Vilajuïga or Garriguella, after a windy night: the vines stand knee-high on their stakes

curiosities:The oldest rock in Catalonia.name: The oldest rock in Catalonia
curiosities:The oldest rock in Catalonia.teaser: The cape's dark rock began as sea mud and ash more than half a billion years ago
curiosities:The oldest rock in Catalonia.story: The dark, layered rock of Cap de Creus started out as mud, sand and volcanic ash on an ancient sea floor, at the turn of the Precambrian and the Cambrian. Volcanic layers inside it have been dated to about 560-540 million years ago, and a gneiss nearby to about 553 million. Around 300 million years ago the collision that raised a mountain chain across Europe buried, heated and squeezed it into schist, and partly melted it at Tudela; bands where the rock was sheared into thin stripes run across the cape. The Gran Enciclopèdia Catalana calls it the most complete series of old rocks in the Catalan lands.
curiosities:The oldest rock in Catalonia.why: Run a hand over a shear band at Tudela: the stripes are a mountain range's worth of pressure, frozen.
facts: The Paratge de Tudela, on the north side of the cape, where the walk to the lighthouse starts (its own card under Walks)

curiosities:Did the vine land at Empúrie.name: Did the vine land at Empúries?
curiosities:Did the vine land at Empúrie.teaser: Local lore says the Greeks brought the vine ashore at Empúries; the archaeology points further south
curiosities:Did the vine land at Empúrie.story: Stand on the beach at Empúries and someone will tell you that wine came to Spain here, carried by the Greek traders who founded Emporion in the 6th century BC. It is a good story and a stubborn one. The digs of recent decades tell another. Phoenician merchants were trading along the Andalusian coast by the 8th century BC, and wine and the vine came with them; by the first half of the 6th century BC, local people at the Alt de Benimaquia near Dénia were already making their own. The Greeks surely traded wine at Empúries. They were probably not first.
curiosities:Did the vine land at Empúrie.why: Drink an Empordà red to the Greeks anyway: they made this gulf a wine port, even if they did not plant the first vine in Iberia.
facts: The amphorae and trade finds at MAC-Empúries; the site has its own card under Culture

curiosities:The Indianos of Begur.name: The Indianos of Begur
curiosities:The Indianos of Begur.teaser: When Begur's cork trade failed, its sons sailed for Cuba and came home rich enough to build palaces
curiosities:The Indianos of Begur.story: In the 19th century Begur lived off cork, and when the cork trade fell into crisis its young men left for the Americas, Cuba above all; one tally puts the emigrants at more than five hundred. Some came back with fortunes and built them into the hill town: tall houses with columned porches, painted walls and gardens behind, some modelled on the mansions of colonial Havana where their owners had lived. Josep Carreras i Frigola, who had gone to Santiago de Cuba in 1831, built the Casa Carreras. In 1870 the returnees opened a Casino for their leisure. The houses still stand along the old streets.
curiosities:The Indianos of Begur.why: Walk the streets below the castle and look up: the porches and painted façades are Havana, built with Begur money.

curiosities:The smugglers' path.name: The smugglers' path
curiosities:The smugglers' path.teaser: The cliff path you walk for the view was cut so armed patrols could watch the coves at night
curiosities:The smugglers' path.story: The camí de ronda, the path that threads along the cliffs from cove to cove, was a patrol route before it was a leisure walk. First the carabineros and then the Guardia Civil walked it to watch the shore for boats landing contraband. The trade peaked in the hungry years after the Civil War, when Spain was short of almost everything: tobacco above all, and also coffee, sugar, medicines and luxuries such as lingerie and make-up came ashore at night. A few smugglers grew rich, and stories of bribed patrols are part of the legend. The path's name means simply the round.
curiosities:The smugglers' path.why: Next time the path squeezes between rock and sea, think of a guard with a lamp at two in the morning.
facts: Any stretch of the camí de ronda; the Calella to Llafranc section has its own card under Walks

larder:Mas Estela.name: Mas Estela
larder:Mas Estela.teaser: Vines among stone terraces in a valley of the Cap de Creus park, farmed by the moon since 1999
larder:Mas Estela.story: The Soto-Dalmau family, Núria and Diego, came to the Sant Romà valley above La Selva de Mar in 1989, bought an old farmhouse and farmed it organically from the first harvest. Ten years later they went biodynamic, working the vines to the lunar calendar with no synthetic inputs; their son Dídac now farms with them. The vines, about sixteen hectares, grow between scrub and dry-stone terraces inside the natural park, picked by hand. Some of the wine rests in clay amphorae. The names to know are Vinya Selva de Mar, Quindals and the two sweet ones, Moscatell Estela and Estela Dolç.

larder:Castell de Peralada.teaser: The appellation's best-known name: a medieval castle, a casino, gardens and a new winery for the visit

The range runs from cava through whites and rosés to the prestige reds and a sweet Garnatxa de l'Empordà. culture:Empúries.name: Ruïnes d'Empúries
culture:Empúries.teaser: A Greek trading town and a Roman city side by side, their streets running down to the sand
culture:Empúries.story: Around 575 BCE Greeks from Massalia landed on this shore and called their trading post Emporion, the market. They first settled the islet that is now the village of Sant Martí d'Empúries, the Palaiapolis, then built the Neapolis on the mainland. In 218 BCE Roman legions landed on this beach to cut off Hannibal, and the conquest of Hispania started there; a Roman town later rose on the slope above. No other site in Spain shows a Greek and a Roman city together. Paths thread between foundations, cisterns and mosaic floors under umbrella pines, and the waves break almost at the edge of the excavations.

craft:Other two.story: For centuries the boats of this coast were built in wood on the beach by the mestres d'aixa, the shipwrights, and caulked by the calafats. craft:What is sold as local craft.name: What is sold as local craft
craft:What is sold as local craft.teaser: A glazed bowl on a beachfront shelf is not La Bisbal pottery until the base says so
craft:What is sold as local craft.story: The souvenir streets of the big resorts, Lloret's front above all, sell the Costa Brava back to its visitors: melting-clock magnets, Dalí moustache mugs, painted bowls labelled Catalan or Mediterranean, and straw bags beside them. A Dalí souvenir is merchandise of a painter, not something made here, and few shops pretend otherwise. The trouble is the vaguer word, handmade, on pottery that names no town and no maker. No published report names a shop here, so read this as advice on reading labels, not a charge against anyone. La Bisbal, inland, is where Empordà clay is actually worked and fired.

drink:The three Garnatxas.name: The three Garnatxas
drink:The three Garnatxas.teaser: Black, white and a dusky pink-grey: one grape family in three skins, and the Empordà bottles all of them
drink:The three Garnatxas.story: On the Empordà plain the old farmers called Garnatxa lledoner, and they grew it in every colour. Garnatxa negra makes most of the reds. Garnatxa blanca gives soft, floral whites. Between them sits lledoner roig, a berry that ripens to a dusty pink-grey and is pressed like a white; the DO Empordà lists it among its white grapes. Of roughly 61 hectares of it in Catalonia, about 60 grow here, so a bottle of it is close to a local exclusive. The vines are low bushes, many of them 50 to 120 years old, which give small crops of concentrated fruit.
drink:The three Garnatxas.why: Order a lledoner roig white once this week: you will rarely meet it bottled on its own anywhere else.
facts: Negra: ripe red fruit, warmth, a little spice. Blanca: white flowers and fennel. Roig: weight, texture and a salty edge, sometimes faintly oxidative

drink:Carinyena.name: Carinyena
drink:Carinyena.teaser: Samsó to the old growers: the black grape that gives an Empordà red its grip and its acidity
drink:Carinyena.story: Carinyena is the second black grape of the Empordà, and on old farms it is still called Samsó. Its vines are tough, drought-proof bushes that crop little and hold their acidity through a hot August, which is exactly what Garnatxa lacks. In the old vineyards the two were planted side by side and picked together, and many Empordà reds are still a blend of both. Phylloxera wiped out the region's vines from 1879; the replanting that followed kept Carinyena in the mix. On its own it tastes of black cherry and bramble, with firm tannin and a sharp, food-friendly edge.
drink:Carinyena.why: Pick a Carinyena-led red when the table orders grilled meat or a black rice; its acidity cuts the fat.
facts: Dark fruit, black cherry and bramble; firm tannin and bright acidity; old vines add depth

drink:Garnatxa de l'Empordà.name: Garnatxa de l'Empordà
drink:Garnatxa de l'Empordà.teaser: Grapes shrivelled by sun and north wind, stopped with spirit, then left in old casks for years
drink:Garnatxa de l'Empordà.story: This is the glass an Empordà farmhouse poured at the end of Sunday lunch. Pale Garnatxa, mostly the red-skinned roja with some blanca, is left on the vine or in the sun until the tramuntana has dried the berries to near-raisins. The must is so sweet that the makers halt fermentation with wine spirit, keeping the sugar in; strengths run from about 14 to 20 per cent, and one Perelada bottling sits at 15. The long-aged ones spend years in old barrels, slowly oxidising until they go amber and taste of dried fig, walnut and toffee. It has nothing in common with the dry reds of the same grape.
drink:Garnatxa de l'Empordà.why: Drink it with a hard sheep's cheese or carquinyolis biscuits, not with a fruit dessert.
facts: Amber to mahogany; dried fig, raisin, walnut, toffee; the older, the more oxidative

drink:Cremat.name: Cremat
drink:Cremat.teaser: A clay bowl of rum on fire at the table, put out with coffee and ladled hot into small cups
drink:Cremat.story: The name just means burnt. Into a wide earthenware cassola go dark rum, sugar, a cinnamon stick, a curl of lemon peel and a few roasted coffee beans. Someone puts a match to it, and for several minutes the blue flame is stirred, lifted on the ladle and poured back, caramelising the sugar while part of the alcohol burns away. A jug of hot coffee goes in to kill the fire. What is left is served scalding in little cups: sweet, smoky, bitter at the edges. The rum is the trace of the nineteenth-century trade between this coast's ships and Cuba.
drink:Cremat.why: Have it lit at your own table on a cool night; the flame is half the drink.
facts: Hot and sweet: burnt sugar, coffee, cinnamon and lemon, the rum softened by the burning

drink:Ratafia.name: Ratafia
drink:Ratafia.teaser: Unripe walnuts and garden herbs steeped in spirit: the dark, bittersweet glass after a long lunch
drink:Ratafia.story: Ratafia begins in early summer, when the walnuts are still green and soft enough to cut through, shell and all. They go into spirit with herbs and spices, and every family keeps its own list; at home the jars traditionally sit out in sun and dew for about forty days. The protected version, IGP Ratafia Catalana, is stricter: at least three months of maceration, then at least three more in wood, and a botanical mix that must include lemon verbena, cinnamon, clove and nutmeg. It comes out dark brown, sweet and slightly tannic from the walnut skins, at 24 to 30 per cent.
drink:Ratafia.why: Ask whether the house pours its own: a village ratafia from a plain bottle is often the best one on offer.
facts: Dark brown; green walnut, clove, cinnamon, herbs; sweet, with a bitter, drying finish

around:Besalú.story: Besalú announces itself from the road: a long Romanesque bridge kinked in the middle, with a gate tower halfway across, carrying you over the river Fluvià into the medieval town. Behind the stone streets lies the old Jewish call. In 1964 the town found, close to the river, a twelfth-century mikveh, a vaulted ritual bath fed by groundwater, the first found in Spain. You can only go down to it with the short guided visit from the tourist office, which also covers the remains of the synagogue above. The rest of the town is free to walk, best before the coaches arrive.

around:Olot and the Garrotxa volcanoes.teaser: Grassed-over cones, a beech wood growing on old lava, and a town that cooks from volcanic soil
around:Olot and the Garrotxa volcanoes.story: Behind Olot the land is pocked with about forty extinct volcanoes, protected since 1985 as the Zona Volcànica de la Garrotxa natural park. Most look like wooded hills until you notice the shape. Santa Margarida hides a perfect round crater with a small Romanesque chapel on the meadow at its floor. Croscat, the youngest cone on the Iberian peninsula, was quarried for its red gravel, which left a cut-away cross-section of the volcano. Between them the Fageda d'en Jordà, a beech wood, grows on a flat lava flow at about 550 metres, gold and copper in late October. Olot's kitchens build their menus from this soil's beans, buckwheat and pork.

avoid:The Lloret seafront.story: Lloret de Mar is the Costa Brava most visitors have heard of, and its seafront promenade is built for volume. The front line is a wall of souvenir shops, generic clubs and terraces selling the tourist menú, with a laminated picture of paella and sangria at around €28 (seen Jun 2026). Nothing about it tells you where you are. The town has better corners: the old streets behind the front, and the coves of Fenals and Cala Boadella either side. For eating, though, the honest answer is to move up the coast to the working fishing ports, where the boats unload what the kitchens cook.

A Catalan arròs is cooked to order and takes its time, so a kitchen that can serve one in ten minutes is telling you something. The urchin weeks of the garoinada run in winter (16 January to 29 March in 2026), spring brings calm water and empty paths, and autumn, where we are now in October, still has warm sea, harvest in the vineyards and room on the terraces. avoid:Urchins out of season.teaser: Sea urchin on a July menu: the roe is thin after spawning, and the local gathering season is closed
avoid:Urchins out of season.story: The violet urchin, garoina on this stretch of coast, is a winter food. Its roe swells through the cold months and peaks around February and March, which is why Palafrugell's garoinada runs from January to the end of March. After the spring spawning the five orange tongues inside shrink to watery threads. Catalonia also regulates the harvest: Ordre ARP/105/2020 sets a management plan for professional gatherers and a closed season for recreational divers, and a 3Cat report gives the permitted window as 1 October to 31 March. An urchin offered in high summer did not come off these rocks legally that week.
avoid:Urchins out of season.why: Save urchins for a winter visit and ask for them raw on toasted bread.

follow:Visit Palafrugell.name: Visit Palafrugell
follow:Visit Palafrugell.teaser: Palafrugell's own tourist office: the garoinada dates and the three coves of Calella, Llafranc and Tamariu
follow:Visit Palafrugell.story: Palafrugell runs its coast as one municipality: the inland town plus the coves of Calella, Llafranc and Tamariu. Its tourist office site is where the garoinada, the winter urchin campaign, publishes its dates and its list of taking-part restaurants each year, and where the Cantada d'Havaneres notices appear. It also lists beach services, parking and the camí de ronda between the coves. When a date in this guide says 'confirm', this is usually the page to confirm it on.
follow:Visit Palafrugell.why: Look here in December for the next garoinada's dates and restaurant list.
facts: Garoinada dates and restaurants, the Cantada notices, the three coves

follow:DO Empordà.name: DO Empordà
follow:DO Empordà.teaser: The appellation's own register of wineries, with the visits you can book among them
follow:DO Empordà.story: The Consell Regulador of the DO Empordà keeps the official list of its member wineries, from the big estates to small family cellers in the Albera hills and on Cap de Creus. Its site is the place to check whether a bottle is from inside the appellation, and to find which cellars open for visits and tastings and how to book them. The DO's own listings are where this guide found the visit prices for several larder cards. Use it to build a wine afternoon on the plain without guessing who opens.
follow:DO Empordà.why: Search it by village before a drive inland to see who takes visitors that day.
facts: The regulatory council of the Empordà wine appellation

follow:El Celler de Can Roca.name: El Celler de Can Roca
follow:El Celler de Can Roca.teaser: The Girona restaurant's own channels: the place to watch for when the next booking window opens
follow:El Celler de Can Roca.story: A table at El Celler de Can Roca is booked months ahead, and the restaurant releases them in batches. Its website and Instagram account, @cellercanroca, are the most reliable signal of when the next window opens, ahead of any agency or concierge rumour. They also carry the news from the family's other places in Girona, such as the Rocambolesc ice-cream shops. The restaurant itself, and the story behind it, has its own card in the tables.
follow:El Celler de Can Roca.why: Follow it from the moment your dates are fixed; set a reminder for the opening day.
facts: The official website and Instagram of El Celler de Can Roca, Girona

follow:Njoy Costa Brava.name: Njoy Costa Brava
follow:Njoy Costa Brava.teaser: An English-language blog on the coast's larder: its cheeses, its urchins and the people who make them
follow:Njoy Costa Brava.story: Njoy Costa Brava is a locally written blog in English that goes deeper into the province's food than the tourist boards do. Its posts cover the small cheese makers of the Empordà, the urchin season, and other products of the coast and the hinterland, the kind of detail a chef looking for suppliers or a guest curious about a plate would want. It is a personal site rather than an official one, so treat opening hours there as a lead to check.
follow:Njoy Costa Brava.why: Read its product posts before a provisioning run; they name the makers.
facts: An independent English-language blog on Costa Brava food and products
